notice: Provisional collection. Records identify reported findings and their limits. The Commons has not independently verified the underlying claims; inclusion is not endorsement.

evidence.title: Retraining can converge under bounded assumptions rather than inevitably amplify instability
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: The authors establish conditional convergence to a stable model when the induced distribution and loss meet stated sensitivity, smoothness and convexity assumptions. Counterexamples diverge when assumptions fail. Observation period and measurement context: Formal analysis and illustrative experiments; no longitudinal field sample.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; Formal analysis; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition

source_locations.SRC-131: Proceedings introduction and §3; v4 §3.2, Theorem 3.5 and Proposition 3.6

evidence.limitations: These assumptions need not hold in deployed ecosystems. Stability does not imply social desirability or global optimality. Proofs and code were not independently checked by the Commons.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Counterconditions qualify universal runaway-feedback claims.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Feedback amplification
terms.definition: A feedback effect in which an activity and the reactions it generates increase the intensity, reach, amount, or consequences of subsequent activity. Stabilizing or dampening responses may limit or reverse amplification.

terms.name: Mechanism hypothesis
terms.definition: A provisional explanation specifying how certain conditions, activities, or relationships could produce an observed or anticipated effect. A useful hypothesis names evidence that could support, qualify, or weaken the explanation.
